summary: Anwar Raslan, a former colonel in the Syrian intelligence services, was convicted of crimes against humanity including murder of 27 persons, torture of at least 4,000 detainees, sexual assault, and deprivation of liberty. The trial, which began in April 2020, was the world's first criminal trial addressing state-sponsored torture by the Assad regime. The court found that Raslan supervised Branch 251 of the General Intelligence Directorate in Damascus between April 2011 and September 2012, where systematic torture and killings occurred. The judgment was a landmark in international criminal justice, demonstrating the potential of universal jurisdiction to address atrocities where territorial courts cannot act. Witness testimony from survivors was central to the prosecution's case. The verdict was upheld on appeal by the Federal Court of Justice in 2023.

The case was the result of a decades-long campaign by victims and human rights organizations, particularly Human Rights Watch and the Association of Victims of Crimes of the Habré Regime (AVCRHH). The conviction was upheld on appeal in 2017. The case established important precedent regarding head-of-state immunity and the obligation to prosecute or extradite under the Convention Against Torture.

The company allegedly paid millions of euros to armed groups, including ISIS, to keep its Jalabiya cement plant operational during the Syrian conflict. In 2019, the Court of Cassation confirmed that a corporation can be charged with complicity in crimes against humanity under French law — a groundbreaking decision. Several former Lafarge executives have also been indicted. The case is the first time a major multinational corporation faces charges of complicity in crimes against humanity, setting a historic precedent for corporate accountability in conflict zones.

summary: The MH17 trial concerned the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 over eastern Ukraine on July 17, 2014, killing all 298 people on board. Three defendants — Igor Girkin, Sergei Dubinsky, and Leonid Kharchenko — were convicted in absentia of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. A fourth defendant, Oleg Pulatov, was acquitted. The court found that a Buk missile system was transported from Russia to eastern Ukraine and used to shoot down the passenger aircraft. The case was prosecuted under Dutch law as 196 of the 298 victims were Dutch nationals. The trial demonstrated the application of passive personality jurisdiction for mass atrocities.

summary: Hamid Noury, a former Iranian prison official, was convicted by the Stockholm District Court for his involvement in the mass execution of political prisoners in Iran in 1988. The trial was groundbreaking as the first international prosecution related to the 1988 prison massacres. Noury was arrested at Stockholm Arlanda Airport in November 2019 based on an arrest warrant. The court found that Noury actively participated in the executions at Gohardasht prison. The conviction was upheld on appe by the Svea Court of Appeal (19 December 2023) and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal (6 March 2024). Noury was released via a prisoner swap with Iran in June 2024 before serving his sentenceal. The case was a landmark in accountability for the 1988 massacres, which Amnesty International has described as crimes against humanity, and demonstrated the reach of universal jurisdiction even decades after events. In June 2024, after the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal, Noury was released and returned to Iran in a prisoner exchange between Sweden and Iran.

summary: This civil case under the Alien Tort Statute (ATS) and Torture Victim Protection Act (TVPA) held former Salvadoran Air Force Captain Alvaro Rafael Saravia liable for the 1980 assassination of Archbishop Óscar Romero. The court found that Saravia acted under the direction of Roberto D'Aubuisson and organized the logistics of the assassination. CJA (Center for Justice and Accountability) represented the plaintiff. The $10 million default judgment, while largely symbolic, established a judicial record of the facts surrounding Romero's murder and demonstrated how civil universal jurisdiction under U.S. law can serve as an accountability mechanism for gross human rights violations committed abroad.

summary: The landmark Filártiga v. Peña-Irala case established civil universal jurisdiction in the United States under the Alien Tort Statute (ATS). The Second Circuit held that the ATS provides federal jurisdiction for civil suits brought by aliens for torts committed in violation of the law of nations. Joelito Filártiga was tortured and killed in Paraguay by Inspector General Peña-Irala in retaliation for his father's political opposition. CCR (Center for Constitutional Rights) brought the case after Peña-Irala was found living in New York. The decision opened the door for decades of human rights litigation in U.S. courts and is considered the foundational case for civil universal jurisdiction.

Despite the dismissal, the case prompted a parallel proceeding in the Netherlands and remains a key reference in corporate accountability litigation.

As prefect, he had authority over local administrators and security forces in a province where some of the worst massacres occurred, including at Murambi school where approximately 50,000 Tutsi were killed. He had been living in France since 1997. The CPCR filed the initial complaint.
key_legal_findings: Prefect-level accountability | Administrative complicity in genocide | Murambi massacre | 20-year sentence for complicity

crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide; Complicity in crimes against humanity
summary: Claude Muhayimana, a Franco-Rwandan bus driver living in Rouen since 1999, was convicted of complicity in genocide and crimes against humanity for transporting Interahamwe militiamen to massacre sites on the hills of Karongi, Gitwa and Bisesero (Kibuye prefecture) during the 1994 genocide. First convicted in December 2021 (14 years), his conviction was confirmed on appeal on March 2, 2026, by the Paris Cour d'assises. He was acquitted of direct participation charges. The appeal motivation letter provides detailed analysis of witness testimony, expert historians, and the establishment of the genocide in the Kibuye region.

crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity
summary: Father Wenceslas Munyeshyaka, a Catholic priest from Kigali's Sainte-Famille church, was accused of genocide and crimes against humanity during the 1994 genocide. Despite extensive evidence, including an ICTR indictment transferred to France, investigating judges issued a non-lieu (dismissal). The case was highly controversial and criticized by human rights organizations and the Rwandan government. It exemplified the early difficulties of French universal jurisdiction proceedings for Rwanda.
key_legal_findings: Non-lieu despite ICTR transfer | Controversial dismissal | Catholic Church involvement | Early French UJ limitations

crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity
summary: Callixte Mbarushimana, former executive secretary of the FDLR (Forces démocratiques de libération du Rwanda), is under investigation in France for genocide and crimes against humanity. He had previously been arrested and transferred to the ICC for DRC-related crimes but was released due to insufficient evidence. The French investigation focuses on his alleged role during the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
key_legal_findings: FDLR leadership accountability | Post-ICC French prosecution | Genocide charges

crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity
summary: Fabien Neretse (alias Fabien Nsabimana) is under investigation in France for genocide. Separately, he was convicted in Belgium in 2023 and sentenced to 25 years for his role in the genocide. The parallel proceedings illustrate multi-jurisdictional accountability for Rwanda.

crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide; Complicity in crimes against humanity
summary: Agathe Kanziga Habyarimana, widow of assassinated Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana, was accused of complicity in genocide for her alleged role in the Hutu Power movement and planning of the genocide. She had lived in France since 1998 under asylum. Despite complaints from CPCR, investigating judges issued a non-lieu. The case was significant for its political dimensions and the debate over the role of the Habyarimana family in the genocide.
key_legal_findings: Presidential family accountability | Hutu Power leadership | Non-lieu — evidentiary challenges

crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide; Complicity in crimes against humanity; Complicity in war crimes
summary: BNP Paribas is under investigation for complicity in the 1994 Rwandan genocide following a complaint by Ibuka France and Sherpa. The bank allegedly facilitated a $1.3 million transfer in June 1994 to a Swiss arms dealer, which was used to purchase weapons for the interim Rwandan government during the genocide. The case represents one of the most significant corporate accountability proceedings for the Rwandan genocide.

case_name: Banque de France (Rwanda — Complicity in Genocide)
crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide; Complicity in crimes against humanity
summary: CPCR filed a new complaint against the Banque de France for complicity in the Rwandan genocide, alleging that the institution facilitated financial transactions that supported the genocidal regime. crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity
summary: Pierre Kayondo was referred to the Paris Assize Court for trial on genocide and crimes against humanity charges related to the 1994 Rwandan genocide. He is among the latest in a series of suspects living in France to be sent to trial by the OCLCH and PNAT.
key_legal_findings: Latest French Rwanda referral | OCLCH ongoing investigations

crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide; Complicity in crimes against humanity; Rape
summary: Investigation into alleged crimes committed by French military personnel during Opération Turquoise in Rwanda (June-August 1994). Complaints include allegations of complicity in genocide through failure to protect Tutsi refugees, and sexual violence against Rwandan women. The case is politically sensitive as it directly implicates the French military's role during the genocide and is linked to broader questions about France's responsibility.

crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide; Complicity in crimes against humanity
summary: Investigation into the alleged delivery of French arms to the Rwandan government during the 1994 genocide, despite an international arms embargo. Complaints allege that French officials authorized weapons transfers that directly facilitated the genocide. The case is part of the broader accountability efforts regarding France's role during the Rwandan genocide.

crimes_charged: War crimes; Genocide
summary: The 'Butare Four' trial was the first case in which a Belgian court convicted persons for crimes committed abroad under international law. The four defendants — Vincent Ntezimana (university professor, 12 years), Alphonse Higaniro (SORWAL factory director, 20 years), and Benedictine nuns Sister Gertrude (Consolata Mukangango, 15 years) and Sister Kizito (Julienne Mukabutera, 12 years) — were convicted for their roles in massacres in the Butare prefecture. The nuns were found to have helped Interahamwe militiamen identify Tutsi refugees sheltering in their convent. The case established Belgian courts as a key forum for universal jurisdiction prosecutions.
key_legal_findings: First Belgian UJ conviction | Religious leaders' accountability | 1993 Belgian UJ law application | Landmark for European UJ

crimes_charged: War crimes; Murder of Belgian peacekeepers
summary: Former Rwandan army Major Bernard Ntuyahaga was convicted for his role in the murder of ten Belgian UN peacekeepers (UNAMIR Blue Helmets) on April 7, 1994, the first day of the genocide. He had been transferred from the ICTR to Belgium for prosecution. The case was significant as it involved Belgian victims and linked the start of the genocide to the murder of peacekeepers protecting Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana.
key_legal_findings: Murder of UN peacekeepers | ICTR transfer to national courts | Passive personality jurisdiction | Start of genocide

crimes_charged: Genocide; War crimes; Murder
summary: Fabien Neretse was convicted by a Brussels Assize Court for genocide and war crimes, including the murder of Belgian nationals, during the 1994 Rwandan genocide. He was found guilty of organizing attacks in the Mataba commune and directly participating in killings. The case was significant as the charges included the murder of Belgian citizens, providing a passive personality jurisdictional basis alongside universal jurisdiction.
key_legal_findings: Belgian nationals murdered in genocide | Combined UJ and passive personality | 25-year sentence

court: Swiss Military Tribunal / Military Court of Appeal
crimes_charged: Murder; Incitement to murder; War crimes
summary: Fulgence Niyonteze, a former bourgmestre (mayor) of Mushubati commune, was the first person convicted under universal jurisdiction for the Rwandan genocide in Europe. He was tried by a Swiss military tribunal, which had jurisdiction over war crimes. Initially sentenced to life, his sentence was reduced to 14 years on appeal. The case predated both the Belgian Butare Four trial and all subsequent European UJ proceedings for Rwanda.
key_legal_findings: First European UJ conviction for Rwanda | Swiss military tribunal jurisdiction | Bourgmestre accountability | Sentence reduced on appeal

case_name: Marie Colvin & Rémi Ochlik (Syria — Deliberate Killing of Journalists)
crimes_charged: War crimes; Crimes against humanity
jurisdictional_basis: Nationality principle (Ochlik was French) + universal jurisdiction
outcome: Ongoing (investigation — 7 arrest warrants issued, incl. Bashar al-Assad)
summary: French judicial investigation into the deliberate shelling of an informal press centre in the Baba Amr district of Homs on 22 February 2012, which killed American journalist Marie Colvin and French photojournalist Rémi Ochlik, and wounded French journalist Edith Bouvier and British photographer Paul Conroy. A joint RSF–SIRAJ investigation (2026) confirmed the strike was premeditated: Assad regime intelligence tracked the journalists' satellite signals, an informant identified the press centre's location, and a strategic meeting of senior military and intelligence officers planned the attack the evening before. A former officer of the 64th Artillery Regiment heard the fire order and the radio confirmation 'the shot is on target.' Seven international arrest warrants have been issued, including against former president Bashar al-Assad and intelligence chief Ali Mamlouk. RSF is a civil party in the proceedings. The case may constitute a crime against humanity as the attack was part of a widespread crackdown on civilians and targeted journalists for their reporting.
key_legal_findings: Deliberate targeting of journalists as war crime | Crimes against humanity — persecution of press | Nationality-based jurisdiction (French victim) | International arrest warrants for heads of state | Premeditated military targeting of civilian press centre
ngos: RSF — Reporters Without Borders (https://rsf.org); SIRAJ — Syrian Investigative Reporting for Accountability Journalism (https://sirajsy.net)

court: Paris Judicial Court (Pôle crimes contre l'humanité)
crimes_charged: Torture; Acts of barbarism
summary: Complaint filed by a victim against Khaled N. for acts of torture and barbarism committed in Algeria. The case was classified without follow-up (classé sans suite) under the French universal jurisdiction framework based on the Convention Against Torture (Régime 2 — art. 689-1 CPP).

court: Paris Judicial Court (Pôle crimes contre l'humanité)
crimes_charged: Torture; Acts of barbarism
summary: NGO and victim complaint against Hocine M. and Abdelkader M., members of pro-government militias in Relizane, Algeria, accused of torture and acts of barbarism. After investigation, the case resulted in a non-lieu (no case to answer) under the Convention Against Torture framework.
key_legal_findings: Convention Against Torture — universal jurisdiction | Non-lieu

case_name: Paul Aussaresses (Algeria — French Torture during Algerian War)
crimes_charged: Crimes against humanity
summary: NGO and victim complaint against French General Paul Aussaresses for crimes against humanity committed during the Algerian War, based on his own public admissions of torture and summary executions. The French courts refused to open an investigation (refus d'informer). The case highlighted the limits of French jurisdiction over crimes committed during the colonial period.

case_name: Mohammed B.S. & Ahmed A.-A. (Jamal Khashoggi Killing)
court: Paris Judicial Court (Pôle crimes contre l'humanité)
crimes_charged: Torture; Acts of barbarism; Complicity in enforced disappearance
summary: NGO complaint filed in France in connection with the murder and dismemberment of journalist Jamal Khashoggi at the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in October 2018. The complaint targeted Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and intelligence official Ahmed al-Asiri for torture, acts of barbarism, and complicity in enforced disappearance. The case was classified without follow-up.
key_legal_findings: Convention Against Torture — universal jurisdiction | Head-of-state immunity challenges | Classé sans suite

crimes_charged: Arbitrary arrest; Unlawful detention; Torture; Acts of barbarism
summary: French trial of Argentine naval officer Alfredo Astiz for the kidnapping, torture, and murder of two French nuns — Alice Domon and Léonie Duquet — during Argentina's Dirty War (1976–1983). Astiz was convicted in absentia by the Paris Assize Court and sentenced to life imprisonment. Argentina refused to extradite him.

case_name: Assassination of Ung Boun Hor (Cambodia — Khmer Rouge)
crimes_charged: Crimes against humanity; Murder; Torture; Acts of barbarism
summary: Victim complaint concerning the killing of Franco-Cambodian parliamentarian Ung Boun Hor during the Khmer Rouge regime. The complaint charged crimes against humanity, murder, and torture. After investigation, the case resulted in a non-lieu. The suspected perpetrators were not identified.

case_name: Members of the Chilean Military Junta (Operation Condor)
crimes_charged: Arbitrary arrest; Unlawful detention; Torture; Acts of barbarism
summary: Long-running French investigation and trial targeting 15 members and associates of the Chilean military junta, including General Juan Manuel Contreras Sepúlveda (head of DINA), Miguel Krassnoff Martchenko, and Paul Schäfer (Colonia Dignidad). The case concerns the disappearance and torture of French nationals during Operation Condor and the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). Several defendants were convicted in absentia.

case_name: Uyghur Forced Labour (Uniqlo, SMCP, Inditex, Skechers)
crimes_charged: Concealment of crimes against humanity; Concealment of genocide; Aggravated forced servitude; Organized trafficking in human beings
summary: NGO and victim complaint against multinational fashion brands Uniqlo France, SMCP (Sandro, Maje), Inditex (Zara), and Skechers for allegedly profiting from forced labour of Uyghur populations in Xinjiang, China. The complaint charges concealment of crimes against humanity and genocide, aggravated forced servitude, and organized trafficking. This landmark corporate accountability case addresses supply chain complicity in mass atrocities.

crimes_charged: Torture; Acts of barbarism; Enforced disappearance; Crimes against humanity
summary: Case concerning the forced disappearance of over 350 Congolese refugees returning from the DRC in 1999 via the Beach river port in Brazzaville. They were arrested by security forces and never seen again. NGO complaints in France targeted Congolese officials under the Convention Against Torture framework. The case resulted in acquittal due to insufficient evidence.

crimes_charged: Complicity in torture; Complicity in enforced disappearance
summary: French tech company Nexa Technologies (formerly Amesys) is accused of selling surveillance technology to the Egyptian regime, which was used to identify, track, and target dissidents who were subsequently tortured or forcibly disappeared. The case was brought by FIDH and LDH. This is a landmark corporate complicity case linking digital surveillance exports to grave human rights violations.
key_legal_findings: Corporate complicity — surveillance technology | Convention Against Torture — universal jurisdiction | Digital surveillance and human rights

crimes_charged: Crimes against humanity; Torture; Complicity in crimes against humanity
jurisdictional_basis: Active personality (art. 113-6 CP) + Universal jurisdiction (art. 689-2 CPP)
summary: NGO complaint concerning 'Opération Sirli', a French military intelligence operation in Egypt. According to investigative journalists, French intelligence provided targeting data to Egyptian forces used for extrajudicial killings of civilians rather than counter-terrorism. The complaint was classified without follow-up.
key_legal_findings: Active personality principle | Military intelligence cooperation | Classé sans suite

court: Paris Judicial Court (Pôle crimes contre l'humanité)
crimes_charged: Arbitrary detention; Torture; Acts of barbarism
summary: NGO and victim complaint against Ahmed Nasser al-Raisi, a senior UAE security official and Interpol president candidate, for his alleged responsibility in acts of torture and arbitrary detention in the UAE. The complaint was filed under the Convention Against Torture while al-Raisi was on French territory for the Interpol General Assembly.
key_legal_findings: Convention Against Torture — presence on territory | Interpol governance and human rights

case_name: Donald Rumsfeld (USA — Abu Ghraib & Guantánamo Torture)
crimes_charged: Torture; Acts of barbarism
summary: NGO complaint against former US Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld for torture at Abu Ghraib and Guantánamo Bay, filed during his visit to France. Based on the Convention Against Torture framework. The case was classified without follow-up.

crimes_charged: Torture; Acts of barbarism
summary: Victim complaint by French nationals Nizar Sassi and Mourad Benchellali, detained at Guantánamo Bay, against George W. Bush and other US officials for torture during their detention. Filed under passive personality jurisdiction (French victims). The investigation resulted in a non-lieu.
key_legal_findings: Passive personality jurisdiction | Guantánamo detention | Non-lieu

crimes_charged: Arbitrary detention; Torture; Unlawful detention; War crimes
summary: NGO complaint concerning CIA extraordinary rendition flights transiting through French territory, transporting detainees to black sites for torture and arbitrary detention. The complaint also alleged violations of the Third Geneva Convention. Classified without follow-up.

court: Paris Judicial Court (Pôle crimes contre l'humanité)
crimes_charged: War crimes; Assassination in connection with terrorism
summary: French prosecution of Ahmed H. for participation in the Camp Speicher massacre near Tikrit, Iraq (June 2014), in which ISIS killed approximately 1,700 Shia Iraqi Air Force cadets. Prosecuted under Régime 3 (art. 689-11 CPP) — one of the first cases applying the 2010 universal jurisdiction law requiring habitual residence in France.

crimes_charged: Complicity in murder; Complicity in attempted murder; Receiving proceeds of crime
summary: Victim complaint against French companies Protec SA, De Dietrich, and Carbone Lorraine (now Mersen) for allegedly supplying chemical weapons precursors to Saddam Hussein's Iraq, used in the 1988 Halabja massacre of Kurdish civilians (~5,000 killed). This corporate accountability case links industrial exports to genocide-level atrocities.

court: Paris Judicial Court (Pôle crimes contre l'humanité)
crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity; War crimes
summary: French investigation opened by the PNAT concerning the August 2014 ISIS massacre of Yazidi populations in the Sinjar region of Iraq. Covers genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes including mass killings, sexual slavery, and forced conversions. Structural investigation opened proprio motu by the prosecution.

case_name: Ahmed E. A. — Camp Speicher Massacre (Iraq/ISIS)
court: Paris Judicial Court (Pôle crimes contre l'humanité)
crimes_charged: War crimes; Terrorism-related killings; Crimes against humanity
summary: French prosecution of Ahmed E. A. for participation in the Camp Speicher massacre near Tikrit (June 2014), in which ISIS killed ~1,700 Shia Iraqi Air Force cadets. Charged with war crimes including use of prohibited methods of combat and inhumane treatment, as well as terrorism-related assassination.

court: Higher Regional Court of Frankfurt am Main
crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity; War crimes; Enslavement; Torture
specialized_unit: ZBKV (Central Office for Combating War Crimes)
summary: The defendant, an Iraqi national and head of an IS office, was found guilty of genocide against the Yazidi religious group. He bought a Yazidi woman and her 5-year-old daughter as slaves. He tied the child to a window grille in extreme heat, causing her death by heatstroke. This was the world's first conviction for genocide against the Yazidi people. The judgment established that IS's treatment of Yazidis constituted genocide.

crimes_charged: War crimes; Unlawful deprivation of liberty; Cruel and inhuman treatment; Torture; Killing
summary: The defendant was found guilty of violating international humanitarian law during Ethiopia's 'Red Terror' period. As a representative of the Derg regime, he committed unlawful deprivation of liberty, cruel and inhuman treatment of hundreds of individuals, and torture and killing of 75 persons during the civil war between the Derg military regime and opposition groups. He was sentenced to life imprisonment.

crimes_charged: War crimes; Cruel and inhumane treatment; Arbitrary detention
summary: The defendant, an Afghan national in charge of a section of the Pul-e-Charkhi prison where political prisoners were held in the 1980s, was living in the Netherlands under a false name. The court found he co-perpetrated humiliating, degrading, cruel and inhumane treatment and arbitrary detention of political prisoners during a non-international armed conflict in Afghanistan.

crimes_charged: War crimes; Prohibited methods of warfare; Attack against civilian population
summary: The defendant, a Syrian member of the 'Free Palestine Movement' militia siding with the Assad regime, fired a portable anti-tank weapon into a civilian crowd in the Yarmouk neighbourhood of Damascus. Four persons were killed and two seriously injured. He admitted the act as revenge for his nephew's killing. The court found a clear nexus between the crime and the armed conflict. The Federal Court of Justice upheld the conviction on appeal.
key_legal_findings: Prohibited methods of warfare | Attack against civilian population | Anti-tank weapon against civilians | NIAC nexus established

case_name: Yan Petrovsky / Rusich (Finland — Ukraine War Crimes)
crimes_charged: War crimes; Killing hors de combat soldiers; Mutilation; Outrage upon personal dignity
summary: The defendant, a Russian national and deputy commander of the far-right paramilitary group Rusich, led an ambush in September 2014 in the Luhansk region that killed 22 Ukrainian soldiers. He was convicted of killing wounded soldiers placed hors de combat, mutilating bodies, and distributing degrading images on social media. The court established the existence of an international armed conflict in Eastern Ukraine. He was convicted on both direct perpetration and superior responsibility grounds.

crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity; War crimes; Enslavement; Forcible transfer of children
summary: The Stockholm District Court convicted a 52-year-old Swedish national of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity — the first conviction in Sweden for crimes against humanity. It is also the first judgment worldwide confirming genocide through the underlying act of forcible transfer of children from one group to another. The case concerned the persecution and enslavement of Yazidi women and children by IS.

case_name: Ahmad Al-K. (Netherlands — Syria War Crime Killing)
crimes_charged: War crimes; Killing of a protected person
summary: A Syrian national residing in the Netherlands was sentenced to 20 years for the war crime of killing. He participated in the execution of a captured Syrian military officer — a protected person under IHL. YouTube videos showing the execution constituted central evidence. He was acquitted of membership in a terrorist organisation.

crimes_charged: War crimes; Complicity in recruitment of child soldiers
summary: A Swedish national who travelled with her children to Syria was convicted of complicity in war crimes for failing to prevent her son (aged 12-15) from being recruited and used as a child soldier by IS. The child died during a mission in August 2013. The court found she was aware of and did not object to her son's recruitment.

case_name: Syrian Asylum Seeker (Sweden — Execution of Soldiers)
court: Svea Court of Appeal / Stockholm District Court
crimes_charged: War crimes; Extrajudicial killing of hors de combat soldiers
summary: A Syrian asylum seeker was sentenced to life imprisonment for actively participating in the deliberate extrajudicial killings of seven captured Syrian soldiers (hors de combat) during the Syrian conflict. A YouTube video on which the defendant appeared constituted the central evidence.

crimes_charged: Genocide; War crimes; Murder; Attempted murder; Rape
summary: The defendant ran a garage in Kigali that became a headquarters for the Interahamwe during the 1994 genocide. Tutsis were massacred in and around the garage complex. He was found guilty of genocide and war crimes including wilful killing, attempted murder and rape. The conviction became final after the Court of cassation rejected his appeal on 18 December 2024.

crimes_charged: Complicity in crimes against humanity; War crimes
outcome: Arrest warrant annulled (personal immunity of sitting head of state)
summary: The French Court of Cassation ruled on the legality of an arrest warrant issued against Bashar al-Assad in 2023 for complicity in crimes against humanity and war crimes. The Court held that personal immunity of sitting heads of state is a rule of customary international law, and that war crimes and crimes against humanity do NOT constitute exceptions to personal immunity for heads of state in-office. However, the Court emphasized that personal immunity is temporary and ceases once the head of state leaves office, and that functional immunity cannot be invoked for genocide, CAH, and war crimes.

case_name: Syrian Central Bank Governor — Functional Immunity Ruling (France)
crimes_charged: Complicity in crimes against humanity; Complicity in war crimes; Money laundering
summary: A dual French-Syrian national, former Governor of the Central Bank of Syria, was indicted for complicity in crimes against humanity and war crimes. The Court of Cassation ruled that functional immunity cannot be invoked for genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes — a landmark ruling reinforcing the exception to immunity for the most serious international crimes.

crimes_charged: Crimes against humanity; War crimes; Torture; Enslavement
summary: The Federal Court of Justice affirmed that functional immunity does not protect foreign public officials from prosecution for core international crimes, regardless of rank or status. The Court also addressed enslavement, ruling that it does not need to last for an indeterminate or prolonged period — duration is merely one factor in the overall assessment.

crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity; War crimes; Enslavement
summary: Swedish woman Lina Ishaq was convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity, and gross war crimes for keeping Yazidi slaves while living with ISIS in Syria in 2015. She enslaved Yazidi women and girls, subjecting them to forced labour and degrading treatment. First Swedish conviction for genocide. Spain (Judge Garzón) issued an extradition request and Mexico ordered his extradition in 2003 in a landmark UJ ruling. After years in Spanish custody, Cavallo was extradited to Argentina in 2008 once domestic prosecutions had resumed, and was sentenced to life imprisonment in Argentina in 2011. A foundational case on UJ + multi-state cooperation for past military-junta crimes.
key_legal_findings: Cross-continental UJ extradition (Mexico → Spain → Argentina) | Garzón's broad reading of LOPJ 23.4 (pre-2009 reform) | UJ as catalyst for return of forum to forum delicti commissi
additional_sources: Asser ICD — Cavallo: https://www.internationalcrimesdatabase.org/Case/1080/Cavallo/

court: Supreme Court of the Netherlands (Hoge Raad)
crimes_charged: Torture
jurisdictional_basis: Universal jurisdiction attempted under Torture Convention Implementation Act
outcome: Hoge Raad ruled UJ NOT applicable retroactively to pre-1989 acts; prosecution barred in NL
summary: Landmark Hoge Raad ruling on the temporal scope of universal jurisdiction. The Dutch Supreme Court held that the Torture Convention Implementation Act could NOT be applied to torture committed before its 1989 entry into force in the Netherlands, even if the underlying acts were already prohibited by customary international law. The ruling barred prosecution of Bouterse for the 1982 'December murders' in Suriname and remains a key precedent on the principle of legality (nullum crimen sine lege) in UJ cases.
key_legal_findings: No retroactive application of UJ statutes (nullum crimen) | Limits of customary international law as basis for domestic prosecution | Hoge Raad reversal of Court of Appeal Amsterdam
additional_sources: Asser ICD — Bouterse: https://www.internationalcrimesdatabase.org/Case/834/Bouterse/

crimes_charged: Torture; Hostage-taking
jurisdictional_basis: Universal jurisdiction (Criminal Justice Act 1988, s. 134 — torture; Taking of Hostages Act 1982)
specialized_unit: Metropolitan Police Counter Terrorism Command / War Crimes Team
summary: First British universal jurisdiction conviction for international crimes. Afghan warlord and commander of a Hezb-e-Islami faction convicted by an English jury for torture and hostage-taking committed in Afghanistan between 1991 and 1996. The trial was the first under s. 134 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 and the first to use live video-link evidence from witnesses in Kabul.
key_legal_findings: First UK UJ conviction under s. 134 CJA 1988 (torture) | Live video-link evidence from Afghanistan | Foundation for UK UJ practice
additional_sources: Asser ICD — Zardad: https://www.internationalcrimesdatabase.org/Case/1232/Zardad/

court: District Court of The Hague; Court of Appeal The Hague; Hoge Raad
crimes_charged: War crimes; Torture
jurisdictional_basis: Universal jurisdiction (war crimes — Wet Oorlogsstrafrecht; torture — Implementation Act)
outcome: Life imprisonment (Court of Appeal, 2011) — confirmed by Hoge Raad (2012)
summary: First Dutch UJ conviction relating to the Rwandan genocide. Joseph Mpambara, a Hutu militia member from Mugonero, was prosecuted in the Netherlands because Dutch law (at the time) did not allow genocide UJ for acts predating 2003 — he was therefore convicted for war crimes and torture (the underlying killings of Tutsi civilians). The Court of Appeal increased his sentence to life imprisonment, confirmed by the Hoge Raad in 2012. The case shaped subsequent Dutch UJ statutory reforms.
key_legal_findings: Workaround conviction (war crimes + torture) where genocide UJ was time-barred | Confirmed life sentence by Hoge Raad | Triggered Dutch UJ statute reform
additional_sources: Asser ICD — Mpambara: https://www.internationalcrimesdatabase.org/Case/845/Mpambara/

court: Tribunal judiciaire de Paris — Pôle CCH/CG/CDG (instruction); Cour d'assises de Paris (renvoi)
crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide; Complicity in crimes against humanity
outcome: Renvoyé devant la Cour d'assises de Paris (instruction close)
summary: Cyprien Kayumba, ancien comptable du ministère rwandais de la Défense pendant le génocide de 1994, a été renvoyé devant la Cour d'assises de Paris à l'issue d'une instruction du Pôle crimes contre l'humanité. Il est poursuivi pour complicité de génocide et complicité de crimes contre l'humanité pour son rôle dans le financement et la logistique des massacres. Plainte avec constitution de partie civile portée par le CPCR.
key_legal_findings: Renvoi aux assises pour complicité de génocide | Article 689-11 CPP | Rôle des fonctions civiles dans l'appareil génocidaire
additional_sources: CPCR — Collectif des parties civiles pour le Rwanda (chroniques d'audience, arrêts, lettres de motivation): https://www.collectifpartiescivilesrwanda.fr/proces/ | AFP — Cyprien Kayumba renvoyé devant les assises: https://www.collectifpartiescivilesrwanda.fr/medias/

court: Pôle crimes contre l'humanité, Tribunal judiciaire de Paris
crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity
outcome: Mis en examen — instruction en cours
summary: Ancien chef d'état-major adjoint des Forces armées rwandaises (FAR) sous Habyarimana, mis en examen en France pour génocide et crimes contre l'humanité. Considéré comme l'un des plus hauts gradés militaires rwandais réfugiés en France faisant l'objet d'une procédure pénale. Plaintes portées par le CPCR. La procédure illustre les difficultés des instructions de longue durée pour les hauts responsables présumés du génocide.
key_legal_findings: Compétence universelle (689-11 CPP) | Responsabilité hiérarchique militaire | Instruction longue durée — haut gradé FAR
additional_sources: CPCR — Collectif des parties civiles pour le Rwanda (chroniques d'audience, arrêts, lettres de motivation): https://www.collectifpartiescivilesrwanda.fr/proces/

case_number: Cour d'assises du Bas-Rhin / Cour d'assises de Meurthe-et-Moselle
court: Cour d'assises du Bas-Rhin (1st); Cour d'assises de Meurthe-et-Moselle (appeal)
crimes_charged: Torture (Article 689-2 CPP, Convention against Torture)
outcome: 8 years' imprisonment (1st instance, 2008); increased to 12 years on appeal (2010)
summary: First conviction in France under the universal jurisdiction provisions of the Convention against Torture (CPP Art. 689-2). Former Tunisian vice-consul Khaled Ben Saïd, previously a police chief in Jendouba, was convicted in absentia in 2008 (8 years) and again on appeal in 2010 (12 years) for acts of torture committed in Tunisia in 1996 against Zoulaikha Gharbi. Landmark precedent for French UJ for torture committed abroad against a foreign victim, opened by the Comité pour le respect des libertés et des droits de l'homme en Tunisie and FIDH/LDH.
key_legal_findings: First French UJ conviction for torture (CPP 689-2) | In absentia conviction confirmed on appeal | Diplomatic functions ≠ functional immunity for torture
ngos: FIDH (https://www.fidh.org); Ligue des droits de l'Homme (LDH) (https://www.ldh-france.org); ACAT-France (https://www.acatfrance.fr)

crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide; Complicity in crimes against humanity
outcome: Mis en examen — instruction; renvoi devant la Cour d'assises de Paris (2023)
summary: Ancien sous-préfet de Gisagara mis en examen et renvoyé devant la Cour d'assises de Paris pour complicité de génocide et complicité de crimes contre l'humanité. Le dossier illustre la coopération entre la France et le TPIR (où Ntawukuriryayo avait été condamné en 2010 à 25 ans, peine confirmée en 2011) puis la procédure française subséquente sur d'autres faits.
key_legal_findings: Compétence universelle (689-11 CPP) | Articulation TPIR / juridictions nationales | Sous-préfet — responsabilité hiérarchique civile
additional_sources: Amnesty France — Cartographie compétence universelle: https://competenceuniverselle.amnesty.fr/affaire/dominique-ntawukuriryayo/ | CPCR — Collectif des parties civiles pour le Rwanda: https://www.collectifpartiescivilesrwanda.fr/proces/

crimes_charged: Crimes against humanity; War crimes; Complicity
outcome: Life imprisonment (in absentia) — Ali Mamlouk, Jamil Hassan, Abdel Salam Mahmoud
summary: Trois hauts responsables du régime syrien — Ali Mamlouk (directeur du Bureau de la sécurité nationale), Jamil Hassan (ex-directeur des renseignements de l'armée de l'air) et Abdel Salam Mahmoud (ex-chef des enquêtes de la branche 235) — condamnés par contumace à la réclusion criminelle à perpétuité par la Cour d'assises de Paris le 24 mai 2024. Première condamnation au monde de hauts responsables syriens en exercice pour crimes contre l'humanité, jugée sur la base des disparitions forcées et meurtres de Mazzen Dabbagh et de son fils Patrick (binationaux franco-syriens) en 2013. Procédure portée par le FIDH, la LDH et le SCM (Syrian Center for Media and Freedom of Expression).
key_legal_findings: Première condamnation au monde de hauts responsables syriens en exercice pour CCH | Procès par contumace — méthodologie FR pour crimes systémiques | Article 689-11 + 113-7 CP (victime française)
ngos: FIDH (https://www.fidh.org); Ligue des droits de l'Homme (LDH) (https://www.ldh-france.org); Syrian Center for Media (SCM) (https://scm.bz)

court: Tribunal judiciaire de Paris — Pôle CCH (instruction)
crimes_charged: Complicity in acts of torture
summary: Plainte déposée en 2012 par la FIDH et la LDH contre la société française Qosmos, accusée d'avoir fourni au régime syrien des technologies de surveillance ('Deep Packet Inspection') ayant facilité l'identification et la torture de dissidents. Après près de dix ans d'instruction, un non-lieu a été rendu en septembre 2021, faute d'éléments suffisants caractérisant l'intention de complicité. Une décision-clé sur les limites de la complicité d'entreprise dans la jurisprudence française.
key_legal_findings: Limites de la complicité corporative — exigence d'intention | Premier dossier français visant un fournisseur de technologies de surveillance | Non-lieu — durée d'instruction (9 ans)
ngos: FIDH (https://www.fidh.org); Ligue des droits de l'Homme (LDH) (https://www.ldh-france.org)
additional_sources: Amnesty France — Cartographie compétence universelle: https://competenceuniverselle.amnesty.fr/affaire/qosmos/ | FIDH — Qosmos / Syrie: https://www.fidh.org/fr/themes/mondialisation-droits-humains/

court: Tribunal judiciaire de Paris — Pôle CCH (instruction)
crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide; Complicity in crimes against humanity
jurisdictional_basis: Active personality (French national — CP Art. 113-6) + universal jurisdiction
summary: Plainte avec constitution de partie civile déposée par le CPCR et Survie en juin 2013 contre l'ancien capitaine de la gendarmerie française Paul Barril, ancien membre du GIGN, pour complicité de génocide et complicité de crimes contre l'humanité. Il lui est reproché un 'contrat d'assistance' signé en mai 1994 avec le gouvernement intérimaire rwandais et la fourniture d'armes pendant le génocide. Dossier emblématique sur le rôle d'anciens militaires français au Rwanda et sur les responsabilités individuelles dans le soutien logistique au régime génocidaire.
key_legal_findings: Rôle d'anciens militaires français pendant le génocide | Complicité par fourniture d'armes et conseil militaire | Compétence personnelle active (CP 113-6)

case_name: Haisam Omar Sakhanh (Syria — execution of POWs)
crimes_charged: Grave breach of international humanitarian law; War crime (summary execution of prisoners of war)
summary: Former Syrian rebel commander convicted in Sweden for participating in the summary execution of seven captured Syrian government soldiers in Idlib province in May 2012, documented in a New York Times video. Sweden's first IHL conviction relating to the Syrian conflict. The court held that the captured soldiers qualified as POWs in a non-international armed conflict and that their execution constituted a war crime.
key_legal_findings: Application of Common Article 3 to NIAC | POW status in non-international armed conflict | Universal jurisdiction over war crimes
additional_sources: ICD — Sakhanh: https://www.internationalcrimesdatabase.org/Case/3409/Sakhanh/ | TRIAL International — Sakhanh: https://trialinternational.org/latest-post/haisam-omar-sakhanh/

crimes_charged: Grave breach of international humanitarian law; War crime (torture / inhuman treatment)
summary: Syrian Free Syrian Army fighter prosecuted in Sweden for participating in the beating and abuse of a captured Syrian government soldier in 2012. Evidence based on a mobile-phone video. One of Sweden's earliest convictions for war crimes in the Syrian conflict, applying Common Article 3 and customary IHL to a non-international armed conflict.
key_legal_findings: War crime in NIAC — torture/inhuman treatment | Mobile-phone video as evidence | Joint criminal action
additional_sources: TRIAL International — Droubi: https://trialinternational.org/latest-post/mouhannad-droubi/

court: Cour de justice du Canton de Genève (Chambre pénale d'appel)
crimes_charged: Complicity in murder (7 extrajudicial prison killings)
specialized_unit: Ministère public du Canton de Genève
summary: Erwin Sperisen, former director of Guatemala's National Civil Police and Swiss-Guatemalan dual national, was prosecuted in Geneva for his role in the 2006 extrajudicial executions of seven inmates at the Pavón prison. Initially sentenced to life (2014), reduced to 15 years on retrial after the Bundesgericht annulled part of the conviction. Landmark Swiss active-personality case for international crimes committed abroad by a Swiss national.
key_legal_findings: Active personality jurisdiction (CP 7) | Command responsibility for police operations | Extrajudicial killings as murder under Swiss criminal law
additional_sources: TRIAL International — Sperisen: https://trialinternational.org/latest-post/erwin-sperisen/ | Legal Tools — Sperisen: https://www.legal-tools.org/case/sperisen/

crimes_charged: War crimes (unlawful deprivation of liberty — 13 counts)
summary: Norwegian-Bosnian dual national prosecuted for participation in the unlawful detention and ill-treatment of Serb civilians at the Dretelj camp in 1992. Norway's first post-WWII war-crimes conviction. The Supreme Court ruled on retroactivity, holding that the 2008 Norwegian Criminal Code provisions on war crimes could not apply retroactively to 1992 conduct, but that the underlying conduct was punishable under pre-existing Norwegian criminal law.
key_legal_findings: Non-retroactivity of 2008 war-crimes provisions | Pre-existing criminality under ordinary criminal law | Active personality jurisdiction
additional_sources: ICD — Repak: https://www.internationalcrimesdatabase.org/Case/1245/Repak/

crimes_charged: Complicity in genocide (murder of approx. 2,000 Tutsi at Kibungo)
summary: Rwandan businessman convicted in Norway for organizing and directing massacres in the Kibungo region during the 1994 Rwandan genocide. Norway's first genocide conviction. The Court of Appeal upheld the 21-year sentence imposed by Oslo District Court, applying the ordinary murder provisions of the 1902 Penal Code because the 2008 war-crimes/genocide provisions could not apply retroactively.
key_legal_findings: Genocide conduct prosecuted as murder (non-retroactivity bar) | Universal jurisdiction | Evidence gathered via international cooperation with Rwanda
additional_sources: TRIAL International — Bugingo: https://trialinternational.org/latest-post/sadi-bugingo/

court: Itä-Uudenmaan käräjäoikeus; Helsinki hovioikeus; Korkein oikeus
crimes_charged: Genocide (Rwanda 1994)
outcome: Life imprisonment (final, upheld by Supreme Court)
summary: Rwandan Baptist pastor prosecuted in Finland for organizing and participating in the killing of Tutsi during the 1994 genocide in the Nyakizu commune. Finland's first genocide trial. The court conducted unprecedented hearings on Rwandan soil. The Supreme Court (Korkein oikeus) upheld the life sentence in 2014, confirming Finnish universal jurisdiction over genocide and the admissibility of evidence collected abroad.
key_legal_findings: Universal jurisdiction over genocide | Hearings conducted in Rwanda by Finnish court | Witness evidence collection methodology
additional_sources: ICD — Bazaramba: https://www.internationalcrimesdatabase.org/Case/1208/Bazaramba/ | TRIAL International — Bazaramba: https://trialinternational.org/latest-post/francois-bazaramba/

crimes_charged: Terrorism; Complicity in war crimes (al-Shabaab killings)
outcome: Supreme Court ruling on liability; remitted for retrial
summary: Somali-Norwegian national prosecuted for participating in al-Shabaab attacks in Somalia. The Supreme Court issued a landmark ruling on the criminal liability of foreign fighters for participation in a terrorist organization that conducts war crimes, clarifying the boundary between terrorism offences and IHL violations.
key_legal_findings: Foreign-fighter liability framework | Terrorism vs. war crimes characterization | Active personality jurisdiction

crimes_charged: Genocide
outcome: Life imprisonment (after BGH reversal and retrial)
summary: Former Rwandan burgomaster tried in Frankfurt for orchestrating the Kiziguro church massacre (~400 Tutsi victims, April 1994). The BGH's 2015 landmark ruling reclassified his role from mere aiding to genocidal co-perpetration (Mittäterschaft), and on retrial the OLG Frankfurt imposed a life sentence.
key_legal_findings: Co-perpetration of genocide (Mittäterschaft) | Mobilising and directing killers as genocidal authorship

crimes_charged: War crimes; Complicity in murder; Illegal arms trafficking; Use of child soldiers
summary: Dutch timber tycoon convicted for supplying weapons and logistics to Charles Taylor's forces in exchange for logging concessions, making him complicit in atrocities including mass murder. The first Dutch conviction of a businessman for international crimes; the Hoge Raad upheld the conviction in 2018.
key_legal_findings: Corporate complicity in war crimes | Active personality jurisdiction over Dutch nationals abroad
ngos: Global Witness; Open Society Justice Initiative

case_name: Bernard Ntuyahaga (Rwanda — killing of 10 Belgian UNAMIR paracommandos)
crimes_charged: War crimes; Murder of UN peacekeepers
summary: Rwandan Army major originally indicted by the ICTR, transferred to Belgium after the ICTR Prosecutor withdrew charges. The Brussels Assizes convicted him for ordering the murder of 10 Belgian peacekeepers on 7 April 1994 — the crime that precipitated Belgium's UN troop withdrawal.
key_legal_findings: UJ over war crimes against UN peacekeepers | Transfer from international to national jurisdiction

case_name: Refik Sarić (Bosnia — Dretelj camp, Denmark's first UJ case)
crimes_charged: Torture; War crimes
summary: Bosnian Croat living in Denmark convicted for personally torturing Muslim prisoners of war at the Dretelj detention camp in 1993. Denmark's first extra-territorial prosecution for international crimes and one of the earliest European UJ torture convictions.
key_legal_findings: Earliest European UJ torture conviction post-CAT | Sufficiency of CAT obligations as basis for domestic prosecution

case_name: Duško Cvjetković (Bosnia — first European UJ genocide trial)
crimes_charged: Genocide
outcome: Acquitted (insufficient evidence); OGH affirmed UJ competence
summary: The first person ever tried for genocide in Europe under universal jurisdiction, brought before a Salzburg jury for alleged massacres of Bosniaks in the Foča area in 1992. Despite acquittal on evidentiary grounds, the OGH affirmed Austria's jurisdictional competence under the Genocide Convention — a foundational European UJ precedent.
key_legal_findings: Austrian UJ over genocide under Genocide Convention | First European UJ genocide trial

case_name: Stanislas Mbanenande (Rwanda — Sweden's first genocide conviction)
crimes_charged: Genocide; Gross violation of international law
summary: Swedish citizen of Rwandan origin convicted of leading local militia in multiple massacres of Tutsi civilians in western Rwanda in 1994. The first genocide conviction in Swedish history, relying extensively on Swedish-police field investigations in Rwanda.
key_legal_findings: Swedish UJ over genocide | Cross-border police investigation methodology

crimes_charged: Genocide; Murder; War crimes
summary: Swedish-Rwandan businessman convicted of organising large-scale massacres of Tutsi in Gitarama Prefecture in 1994 and personally shooting victims. Sweden's second genocide conviction; Svea hovrätt upheld life imprisonment in May 2016 and the Högsta domstolen denied leave to appeal.
key_legal_findings: Second Swedish UJ genocide conviction

crimes_charged: Genocide; Gross violation of international law
summary: Örebro resident (who had changed his name from Rukeratabaro) convicted of leading an interahamwe unit that killed hundreds of Tutsi sheltering at a school in Kigali-Rural in April 1994. Sweden's third genocide conviction, notable for the appellate court's on-site evidence-gathering visit to Rwanda.
key_legal_findings: Third Swedish UJ genocide conviction | In situ appellate evidence-gathering in Rwanda

case_name: National Commissioner SAPS v. SALC (Zimbabwe Torture Docket)
crimes_charged: Torture as crime against humanity
jurisdictional_basis: Universal jurisdiction (ICC Implementation Act 27 of 2002; CAT)
outcome: SAPS ordered to open formal investigation (unanimous)
summary: After SAPS refused to investigate a SALC dossier on Zimbabwean state torture of MDC activists, the Constitutional Court unanimously held that South African law and international obligations require investigation of crimes against humanity occurring abroad. A landmark African UJ ruling establishing the duty to investigate as non-discretionary.
key_legal_findings: Duty to investigate CAH abroad is mandatory | ICC Implementation Act read in light of customary international law
ngos: Southern Africa Litigation Centre; Zimbabwe Exiles Forum

case_name: Hissène Habré — EAC Trial Chamber Judgment
crimes_charged: Crimes against humanity; War crimes; Torture; Rape; Sexual slavery
summary: First-instance EAC judgment convicting former Chadian President Habré for atrocities committed during his 1982–1990 rule. The first time an African court applied universal jurisdiction under the AU framework to convict a former head of state, with major rulings on command responsibility, sexual slavery, and individual reparations.
key_legal_findings: UJ conviction of former head of state by African court | Sexual slavery as CAH | Individual reparations award

case_name: Hissène Habré — EAC Appeals Chamber Judgment
crimes_charged: Crimes against humanity; War crimes; Torture; Sexual slavery
outcome: Conviction upheld (life imprisonment); personal rape acquittal
summary: The EAC Appeals Chamber upheld Habré's life sentence for CAH, war crimes and torture while modifying the judgment to acquit him personally of rape and affirming sexual slavery as CAH. The first appellate confirmation of an African head-of-state UJ conviction.
key_legal_findings: Appellate confirmation of UJ conviction of former head of state | Sexual slavery doctrine refined

court: Juzgado Nacional en lo Criminal y Correccional Federal No. 1 (Buenos Aires)
crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity; Enforced disappearance; Torture; Extrajudicial killing
jurisdictional_basis: Universal jurisdiction (Argentine Penal Code; customary international law)
outcome: Ongoing — international arrest warrants and indictments issued; Spain refuses extradition
summary: The only criminal investigation in the world targeting Francoist crimes (1936–1977), opened after Spain's own courts closed relevant proceedings. Judge Servini de Cubría has issued international arrest warrants against former Francoist officials (including ex-Interior Minister Martín Villa) and indicted over 20 suspects. Spain has uniformly refused extradition.
key_legal_findings: Argentine UJ over crimes abroad against non-Argentine victims | Imprescriptibility of CAH and enforced disappearance
ngos: CEAQUA; ARMH; Fundación Internacional Baltasar Garzón

case_name: Abu Omar / Nasr (Italy — CIA extraordinary rendition)
court: Tribunale di Milano / Corte d'appello / Corte di Cassazione
crimes_charged: Kidnapping (sequestro di persona); Complicity in torture
jurisdictional_basis: Territorial (abduction in Milan) + active/passive personality for Italian co-conspirators
outcome: 23 CIA officers + 1 USAF colonel convicted in absentia (7–9 yrs); 2 SISMI officers convicted
summary: Egyptian cleric Hassan Mustafa Osama Nasr (Abu Omar) was seized on a Milan street by CIA and Italian intelligence in 2003 and rendered to Egypt, where he was tortured. The Milan Tribunal's 2009 judgment was the world's first trial of an extraordinary rendition operation; the Cassazione's 2012 ruling upheld most CIA convictions and confirmed that extraordinary rendition constitutes criminal kidnapping.

case_name: Félicien Kabuga (France — arrest and surrender to the IRMCT)
crimes_charged: Genocide; Crimes against humanity
jurisdictional_basis: Territorial arrest / cooperation with international mechanism

The Cour de cassation rejected his challenge and confirmed his surrender to the Mechanism (chambre de l’instruction Paris, 3 June 2020). The case bridges the national layer and the tribunals layer (IRMCT).

case_name: Yvonne Basebya (Rwanda — Netherlands, incitement to genocide)

case_name: H.S.A. et al. v. Ariel Sharon & Amos Yaron (Sabra and Shatila — Belgium)

The diplomatic storm that followed led to the repeal of the Belgian universal jurisdiction law in August 2003.

crimes_charged: Genocide; War crimes; Torture

crimes_charged: Crimes against humanity (complaint)

summary: Constitutional amparo applying the STC 237/2005 (Guatemala) doctrine of broad universal jurisdiction to the Falun Gong complaint against Chinese leaders — part of the Spanish UJ arc later curtailed by the 2009 and 2014 reforms.

case_name: Simón, Julio Héctor y otros (Argentina — annulment of the amnesty laws)
court: Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación
